draft.title: Simple cubic equations
card: A simple cubic equation has a cube such as \(x^{3}\) and no other power of \(x\). Solve it by isolating \(x^{3}\), then taking the cube root of both sides.
Worked example: \(2x^{3} = 54\). Divide by 2 to get \(x^{3} = 27\). Then \(x = \sqrt[3]{27} = 3\).
A negative number has a real cube root. For \(x^{3} = -8\), the answer is \(x = -2\), because \((-2) \times (-2) \times (-2) = -8\).
Unlike \(x^{2} = 9\), which has two answers, \(x^{3} = k\) has only one real answer. Check by cubing your answer.
draft.remember: Isolate the cube, then take the cube root. There is one real answer.

a.why: Subtract 5 to get \(x^{3} = 8\), so \(x = \sqrt[3]{8} = 2\). The option \(\pm 2\) is wrong because a cube equation has only one real answer: \((-2)^{3} = -8\), not 8.
a.clue: Subtract 5 first, then take the cube root.

b.q: Priya says the cubic \(3x^{3} = -81\) has no real solution because 81 is not negative. What is the correct solution?
b.why: Divide by 3 to get \(x^{3} = -27\). Then \(x = \sqrt[3]{-27} = -3\), since \((-3)^{3} = -27\). Priya is wrong because a negative number does have a real cube root.
b.clue: Divide by 3, then ask which number cubed gives \(-27\).

problems.detail: Priya's reasoning is garbled. The equation gives \(x^{3} = -27\), a negative number, yet she is quoted as saying there is no real solution 'because 81 is not negative'. The why says her error is thinking a negative number has no real cube root, so the stem should say she reasons that \(-81\) (or \(-27\)) is negative.
